analysis: Ushojo ẓigdege pull (past) has a ẓig root and eg past formation; compare a long/stretch derivative only provisionally. Drakk lacks the medial g and does not follow from the gloss; initial stress on the actual form is retained.

Ushojo gaṇḍuli pumpkin is plausibly a round/lump gourd formation related to gaṇḍa rather than latā creeper, but the crop-name transfer and ul/i suffix need lexical evidence. Final stress may be derivational; no old accent is assigned.

SchmidtKaul2008pp247–248 identifies rain charchu, ram chundir, right trangwuṅi, rooster byaapho and shoulder stod as Purik loans, and salt paytshu as Burushaski. Several stored spellings/orderings differ from the source discussion, requiring cell correction. None should be treated as an inherited varṣa, mēṇḍha, dakṣiṇa, kukkuṭa, skandha or lavaṇa reflex.

Ushojo hinaan rainbow may be a reduced deity/bow compound, but neither indradhanus nor śr̥ṅgadrōṇa has an established sound correspondence to its initial hin. Retain final stress and a compound hypothesis without selecting the input to fit it.

Ushojo phagan raspberry may share a phal/phalgu fruit-name element, but a precise old botanical referent and g/n development are unknown. Final stress remains unaccounted for historically; no fig-family assignment is made from ph alone.

Ushojo subʌno right pairs with abʌno left; shared bʌno and contrasting prefixes suggest a synchronic directional pair. This independent morphology is more promising than forcing both into dakṣiṇa/kharva. Their shared medial stress could be a property of the common base, but its etymology remains open.

Ushojo beli roof is not an evident śalākā, tala or śaraṇa reflex. A beam/plank-derived roof term is possible; initial stress and final i are retained pending an independently supported timber etymology.

Brokskat pattaq root differs from both mūla and nāḍī. Regional bottom/base or plant-root vocabulary may explain it, but the final velar and stress require lexical evidence; it remains a replacement in cross-language tables.
Ushojo pare rope does not clearly match rajju, setra, dāman or vāla. A plait/binding derivative or local material name is possible, but no secure ancestral source or accent is established.

Brokskat rilbu round resembles Tibetan ril bu round object/ball, independently different from the piṇḍara round family. Check donor form and adjectival use before a firm loan claim; initial stress is observable as loan-adaptation evidence if confirmed.
Ushojo maṇḍa the run is a noun/adverb plus do construction. The first element needs a running/race etymology; it is not a direct tarp jump verb. Compound stress is not marked in this token.

Stored (thing) ek šei includes English gloss material. The lexical phrase ek šei same thing contains éka one plus a regional thing noun (possibly šai loan). It is a phrase, not a reflex of samá; split before counting its two components.

Brokskat siri sand could be a heavily reduced sikatā derivative but r in place of the medial material requires independent evidence. Do not import Ushojo sigal's family from gloss identity; retain initial stress as an unassigned lexical observation.

Ushojo khaṇ sap is distinct from rasa and jatu and may designate resin/gum rather than generic sap. A material-name etymology needs source semantic clarification; the unmarked monosyllable supplies no historical accent contrast.

Ushojo laṛam scorpion resembles the regional laṛam/lṛam scorpion vocabulary, including neighboring Iranian usage; borrowing is plausible. It is not a regular vṛścika or ṭōṅka reflex and has no secure Old Indo-Aryan accent baseline.

Brokskat paae nakhlis seasonal migration is a multiword event expression with two stresses. It may combine a pasture/spatial element and a motion verb, but no whole-word input should be reconstructed. Preserve both stresses and seek the verb paradigm.

Ushojo dumoŋgo second transparently shares moŋgo with fourth carmoŋgo. The base is two and the ordinal morphology is renewed, so it is not a dulāva twice-reaped reflex despite candidate gloss overlap. Stress belongs to the ordinal base/suffix junction.

Brokskat skis and Ushojo cake see are candidates for a cakṣ/seeing root rather than paśyati, with Brokskat citation s. The apparent c/k/s correspondence is promising but requires full Turner and paradigm comparison before accepting a new family; initial Ushojo stress remains independent evidence.

Ushojo dege ce bi seventy and ce bi sixty are ten plus three twenties and three twenties, respectively. Their compositional structure distinguishes them from inherited saptati/ṣaṣṭi; compare numeral components only after lexical splitting.

Brokskat mys grib shady side contains the Purik grib explicitly identified by SchmidtKaulp248, plus an alternative mys whose relation to shadow/fat homonyms needs the printed punctuation. Do not assign either to apacchāyā by meaning alone.

Ushojo phiṭkarege shake (past) has a phiṭkar stem plus eg past morphology. A burst/flick expressive root with kar extension is possible, but it must be checked against present forms; late stress may belong to the derived stem rather than inherited root accent.

Brokskat tsap tsap sharp is reduplicated and independent of tīkṣṇa/tino. Expressive sound symbolism or a Tibetan/Purik adjectival source are plausible; the doubled word must not be interpreted as two accent positions in one inherited adjective.

Brokskat muley pho she contains the same pho used for he plus a feminine modifier. Its phrasal grammar and possible contact components require separate analysis; it is not a simple feminine sa reflex.

Brokskat stored nilo sheep does not transparently continue ēḍa; printed initial n may be a reading error. Verify the cell before adopting the tempting ēḍa/yilo route; the acute cannot independently license a mora claim.

Ushojo ili female sheep / miṇḍal male sheep contains distinct lexical stems: ili is a plausible ēḍa descendant, while miṇḍal clearly belongs to mēṇḍha with al extension and final stress. These must be split and cannot be counted as accent variants of one etymon.

Ushojo lamor miṇḍal fat-tailed sheep combines a tail adjective with the extended ram noun. The lam component has competing lāṅgūla/lamba/lūma ancestry; both words carry stress, so this is a compound/phrase and not an unextended tail reflex.

Ushojo ḍal shield resembles widespread ḍhāl shield vocabulary, not khēṭa. Transmission and aspiration loss require regional evidence; no inherited accent baseline is assigned from the current candidates.

Ushojo juŋgi ãṭi shin bone is a leg-plus-bone phrase; ãṭi belongs to the aṣṭhi bone set958 while juŋgi is related to the joŋ leg alternative. The first member's stress is phrase-level evidence, not the accent of an old simple shin noun.

Brokskat boṣuṅs sickle is distinct from aṅka, dātra and lavitra. A cutting-tool derivative or regional loan is possible; final s need not be verbal merely because similar citation verbs end in s. Its nominal morphology remains unresolved.

Ushojo ḍug bile sink (past?) combines a sinking/immersed element with become past bile. Compare regional ḍub/ḍug only provisionally; its final stress belongs to the auxiliary and must not be projected onto an old sink root.
Brokskat thuro skin is not an evident carman or chōll reflex. A hide/covering term or contact replacement remains possible; initial stress and final o are retained without a fabricated old formation.

Ushojo baruno skin bag may be a container derivative rather than the material skin noun. Neither māna nor khalla explains the b/r frame; medial stress could be derivational, but no independent source is established.

Brokskat dolo sky is distinct from ākāśa and āsmān. A high/above spatial term nominalized as sky is possible, but the d/l structure requires source lexical evidence; final stress remains an unexplained lexical outcome.
Ushojo ḍoko sledgehammer resembles an expressive striking/tool base and differs from vardhira. Initial stress and final o are documented; its old input is unresolved.

Brokskat saeeeno titaq contains two alternatives: SchmidtKaulp248 identifies saeen(o) as an unidentified Indo-Aryan loan and titaṅ as Purik. The multiple e and final q are reading issues; neither is a direct inherited laghu/cūrṇa reflex.

Ushojo šinoṭo small appears to contain a small/fine ši(n) base plus oṭ/o morphology, potentially related to cūrṇa/čini, but that segmental pathway is not established. Medial stress before final o is consistent with a derived adjective without proving its etymology.

Brokskat dre smoke is not transparently dhūma. A regional vapor/smoke word or contact borrowing may explain it, but no secure donor or old accent has been established; it remains a lexical replacement.
